An Asscher cut diamond is `a square step-cut stone with cropped corners that creates a signature "hall of mirrors" geometric effect`.[[1]](https://www.brilliantearth.com/diamond/asscher/)[[2]](https://www.goodstoneinc.com/collections/asscher-cut)[[3]](https://www.queensmith.co.uk/diamond-guides/diamond-shapes/asscher)

### Key Characteristics

- **Facets:** A standard Asscher cut features 58 wide, linear step facets arranged in concentric squares. (A patented variation, the Royal Asscher, features 74 facets).[[1]](https://www.goodstoneinc.com/collections/asscher-cut)[[2]](https://www.queensmith.co.uk/diamond-guides/diamond-shapes/asscher)[[3]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J3_C3gnLUBg)[[4]](https://www.facebook.com/royalasscherdiamonds/videos/mike-breaks-down-the-difference-between-the-asscher-cut-and-the-royal-asscher-cu/1315256846451309/)
- **Shape:** It has a nearly 1:1 length-to-width ratio, making it a true square with distinctive cropped corners that form an octagonal outline.[[1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J3_C3gnLUBg)[[2]](https://www.goodstoneinc.com/collections/asscher-cut)[[3]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kbxxr92DPhs&t=4)
- **Appearance:** Because of its deep pavilion and high crown, an Asscher cut can face up slightly smaller on the finger than a round or brilliant-cut diamond of the exact same carat weight.[[1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kbxxr92DPhs&t=4)[[2]](https://www.goodstoneinc.com/collections/asscher-cut)[[3]](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DYbis-iJwlf/?hl=en)
- **The 4 Cs Priority:** Because step cuts have large, open tables that do not hide flaws well, **clarity** and **cut** are more vital than color; many buyers select VS1 clarity or higher while dropping slightly on color grades.[[1]](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DYbis-iJwlf/?hl=en)[[2]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J3_C3gnLUBg)[[3]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kbxxr92DPhs&t=4)

### Pricing & Options

- **Price Range:** Loose or set stones generally range from roughly $300 for smaller lab-grown options up to $30,000+ depending heavily on carat size, clarity, and whether the diamond is natural or lab-grown.
- **Popular Retailers:** You can browse options or loose stones through major jewelers like [Blue Nile](https://www.bluenile.com/diamonds/asscher-cut), [Brilliant Earth](https://www.brilliantearth.com/diamond/asscher/) , or [Whiteflash](https://www.whiteflash.com/diamond-education/diamond-shapes/asscher-cut/).[[1]](https://www.bluenile.com/diamonds/asscher-cut)[[2]](https://www.brilliantearth.com/diamond/asscher/)[[3]](https://www.whiteflash.com/diamond-education/diamond-shapes/asscher-cut/)

If you know me by now, you will know I just love antique diamonds in general. Their individuality and brilliance is truly unmatched. 

But to come across an antique Asscher cut diamond of this size is so incredibly rare, I can’t even tell you. 

Stare into those facets and tell me you don’t see natural beauty. This is a 1 of 1 in the world. Can never be replaced or replicated! 

I get asked all the time what my favourite shape is. You have your answer in this video ❤️🤩

Some cuts chase attention.
This one makes you look closer.

4.00ct Asscher.
Underrated. My personal favourite.

With step-cut facets this open, clarity has nowhere to hide.

Framed in my classic halo.
Finished with Italian pavé.

For those who know what they’re looking at.

An 8ct Early Asscher Cut

This is not how most Asscher Cuts look today.
This original early 20th-century example comes from a Boucheron ballerina ring and reflects a very different approach to the shape.

Instead of the flatter profile and larger table seen in many modern Asscher Cuts, this diamond is chunkier, with broader corners, a smaller table and more substantial proportions.

That early construction changes the way the stone handles light. The reflections feel broader, deeper and less graphic than those of a modern version, giving the diamond a heavier, more architectural presence.

The Boucheron setting is impressive, but for me, it almost competes with the stone.

I would rather see this diamond in something simpler—quiet enough to let the proportions, the geometry and the age of the cut do the work.

Sometimes an important diamond needs less around it, not more.

Question: Liz Taylor’s Krupp diamond of 33.19 carats is said to be an asscher cut diamond. Isn’t an asscher cut diamond a square diamond with cut corners? Hers was not. It looked more like an Art Deco emerald cut, meaning it is not like todays emerald cuts.

Joseph Asscher spent weeks mapping the Cullinan diamond before successfully splitting it on his second try. But the lore surrounding that moment is legendary in the jewellery trade.

For ages, the famous story was that the crushing psychological pressure was so overwhelming that the second the diamond sheared in two, Asscher lost consciousness and fainted on the floor of his workshop. 

In reality, his family later admitted the fainting story was a myth. He didn’t pass out. After successfully splitting the most valuable piece of rough diamond in human history, he calmly put down his tools, walked into the next room, and opened a bottle of champagne. What a baller.

But what actually happened to the yield of that historic hammer strike?
